chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Blue Belt
chapters.artPrompt: a sturdy little boy in a coarse grey coat buckling a bright blue belt about his waist on a mountain path, a fleeing giant's shadow among split boulders behind him, northern pine slopes and a silver stream, bright clean light, sturdy cheerful storybook illustration

blocks.text: A widow sent her youngest son out into the world to seek his fortune, as youngest sons do in tales. He walked north till the farms were far behind him. On the road he met an old woman, and helped her carry her bundle without being asked. She watched him go with a smile at her heart. When they parted she gave him a blue belt. “Buckle it round you,” she said, “and you will have the strength of many men.”

Soon after, in a dark wood, a sly old witch asked him in to supper. But he had been warned to be careful with strangers on the road. He thanked her kindly and walked on — and her face behind him was not a kind face at all.
The troll sees the small boy on the path — and the blue belt.

Higher up, a huge troll came striding down the mountainside, and the trees shook at his steps. The boy stood his ground. The troll laughed to see so small a lad, and tore a great rock from the hillside to throw. The boy caught it in both hands — for the blue belt's strength was in him — and dashed it to pieces. The troll turned and fled, and was never seen in that country again.

The small boy with the blue belt was welcome in every valley after that. He lifted what needed lifting and pulled what needed pulling, and never once used his strength to bully. And when people asked where such strength came from, he always said the same thing: from a kind old woman, and a bundle carried politely.
New word: fortune — luck and riches together. Ask your child: the belt gave strength, but what gave the boy his good name?

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Girl Who Trod on a Loaf
chapters.artPrompt: a small child in a red hood kneeling in a snowy lane with a bright tear falling, far away a grey statue-like girl standing deep in a dark marsh below, a little seabird flying up toward a shaft of sunlight, soft white-grey winter light with one warm ray, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: Inge was a poor man's child, and as pretty as a doll, and as proud as a peacock. As she grew up she grew prouder still, and cared for nothing but her fine shoes and her curls. One day she set out across the dark moor, carrying a loaf of new bread. The path grew wet and muddy. Rather than spoil her pretty shoes, she threw the loaf down and set her foot on it, to cross.

But the loaf sank with her, and she sank with the loaf — down, down, into the marsh. She came to the moor-woman's great brewery, and lower still, to a cold grey place where she could not stir a step. There she stood, like a statue, through long, long years, while her story was told in the world above: how the proud girl trod on bread to save her shoes. Everyone who heard it shook their heads.
A little child hears the story of Inge — and weeps a tear of pity.

Then one day the story reached a small child, who cried over it instead of shaking her head. “Poor Inge!” said the child. “She is punished enough. Could no one set her free?” And one tear fell for Inge's sake, and found its way all the way down to the dark place where Inge stood.

The tear turned into light. The light grew till it wrapped Inge round like wings, and something stirred in the stone. Where the proud girl had stood there rose a little grey bird, glad and quick, and it flew up out of the darkness into the sunshine. And in Denmark, when a small sea-bird skims singing over the marshes, people still think of Inge — and of how one tear of kindness opens the heaviest doors.
Talk together: Inge sank for treading on bread, and rose again because a child wept for her. Ask your child: what one kind thought changed the whole story?

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Magician's Horse
chapters.artPrompt: a thin young stable-boy leaping onto a magnificent dark horse that rears and glows with inner light, the gates of a strange walled garden open behind them, a small dark figure of a magician far off among the hedges, dawn light, sweeping storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was once a great magician, who hired a poor boy to serve in his stables and his garden. The magician was kind in his way, but he had one hard rule: the farthest stable door was never to be opened, not for any reason. “Ask me for anything else,” he said, “and you shall have it.”

The boy served faithfully and asked for nothing. But a locked door is a louder question than any words, and one day his curiosity won. Inside the far stable stood a horse such as he had never seen, splendid and strange, with eyes like lamps. The horse spoke. “You have come at last,” it said. “I have waited long for you. Open my stall, and we shall both be free.”
The wonder horse waits behind the forbidden stable door.

In the grey of morning the boy led the horse out, and they went like the wind. But magicians know their own, and the magician came after them, swift and terrible. “Fear nothing,” said the horse. “Whatever I bid you, throw behind you.” And what the boy threw rose up behind them into walls and mountains, and the pursuit was ended.

The horse brought him to a great city, where no one had ever seen such a rider or such a horse. There the young man won honour in the trials of riding, and a good place at court, and the magician never found a door back into his life. As for the horse, he had grass enough and oats enough, and the gate always open — for a horse who talks is a friend, and friends are not shut in.
New word: curiosity — the wish to know things. Ask your child: was the boy right to open the door? What do you think was behind the magician's rule?

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · Fortunatus and his Purse
chapters.artPrompt: a young traveller in a Renaissance cloak bowing before a glowing Lady Fortune standing on a rolling glass sphere in a moonlit wood, she holds out a fat little purse of gold, two paths part behind him under tall trees, silvery moonlight with gold sparks, romantic storybook illustration

blocks.text: In Cyprus, long ago, there lived a poor young man called Fortunatus, which means lucky. He was not lucky at all, at first. One day, wandering in a wood, he came upon a lady shining like moonrise, standing on a rolling ball. “I am Fortune,” she said. “Choose: riches, wisdom, strength, health, or long life.” Fortunatus chose riches, and she gave him a small purse. “Open it when you will,” she said. “There will always be gold in it.”

The purse never failed him. He crossed the sea, saw the great cities of the world, and made friends everywhere with his open hand. A hundred courts welcomed him, for a man whose purse is open finds doors open too. In his travels he won a second marvel: a wishing hat, that carried him wherever he named, in the winking of an eye.
The purse that never emptied — and the hat that wished the way.

At last Fortunatus married, and had two sons, and told them the story of the wood and the rolling ball. He warned them to be careful with wonders, as careful as he had been. But young men are not always careful.

When he was gone, the sons found the purse, and quarrelled over it, and spent like two lords. They pulled the hat this way and that, each wanting to fly from the other, until neither wonder worked any more. The sons of the lucky man ended poorer than he began, and the wood with the rolling ball was remembered longest of all. And that is why old nurses say: a gift is only as good as the hands that hold it.
Talk together: Fortune offered wisdom as well as riches. Ask your child: which would you have chosen — and what would you do with it?

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Story of Three Wonderful Beggars
chapters.artPrompt: a poor young man and his wife sharing steaming bread with three hooded wanderers at their little table by candlelight, snow drifting past the small window, a humble cottage with a warm fire, gentle golden light, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was once a young man and his wife as poor as autumn leaves, and the sweetest-tempered couple in the whole country. Whatever they had, they shared it. A crust went to the beggar at the gate, a corner of the fire to the traveller, and there was never a grudging word in that little house. That was their whole fortune, and they thought it enough.

One snowy evening came a knock at the door, and there stood three beggars, older than old, with hooded faces. “We are hungry, and far from home,” they said. The couple had bread enough for exactly one supper. They set it steaming before the strangers, and sat by without supper themselves, and were merry all the same. “Come again any night,” said the wife. “There is warmth in this house for everybody.”
Three hooded beggars share the last loaf of the house.

When they rose to go, the three blessed the little house. “Your bread shall never be quite done,” they said, “nor your kettle quite cold, while your door stays open to the poor.” Then the door stood empty, though the night was wild, and no footprints led away into the snow. Only the fire crackled, warmer than before.

And so it was, year after year: there was always a loaf a little more than was needed, and always someone at the door to need it. The couple grew old in that cottage, warm and well, and travellers carried the tale of the three wonderful beggars far and wide, and children in that country learned their sharing on doorsteps, with the three beggars for a bedtime story.
Talk together: the couple gave away their very last loaf. Ask your child: what did the three beggars really leave behind — and what does an open door cost, or give?

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Stan Bolovan
chapters.artPrompt: a jolly big Romanian farmer in a sheepskin vest standing outside a tiny cottage surrounded by a crowd of little children waving, distant stony hills under a warm sunset, hens and a skinny dog among the children's feet, warm comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Once there lived a good man called Stan Bolovan, as poor as winter and as kind as spring. He and his wife had no children, and their one wish was for a house full of them. One day Stan prayed that he might have as many children as there were hairs on his head. Fairy tales warn us to be careful what we wish for. He came home to a cottage full of children — a hundred of them, so the tale says — and his wife stood in the middle, laughing and crying at once.

For a week it was all joy. Then it was all porridge, or no porridge at all. A hundred mouths are hard to fill with not one coin in the house. So Stan kissed his wife, told the children to mind their mother, and set out to find work enough for a hundred.
Stan walks into the stony country, where the dragon's hundred children wait.

Far away in a stony country, Stan was hired — by a dragon, who had a hundred children of his own. Stan kept the little dragons fed and warm, and earned good gold, and kept his eyes open. For he soon saw that there was no love in the dragon, and a nurse must watch as well as work.

When the dragon's temper turned black, Stan's quick wits kept every little dragon safe. And when he had earned wages enough for a hundred bowls of porridge, he said goodbye to the children, slipped away while the dragon slept, and walked home by the straight road. He found his hundred children safe and hungry, and his wife waiting at the door. The tale-tellers ask how a poor man fed a hundred, and the answer is always the same: one bowl, and then the next.
Talk together: Stan asked for a hundred children, and then had to feed them. Ask your child: what would our house be like with a hundred children in it?
